traveler: William the Conqueror (Guillaume le Bâtard, Duke of Normandy and King of England)
title: The Keep at Falaise to the Burst Tomb at Caen: the Bastard, the Crossing, and the Book
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Falaise, birth in the ducal keep
stops.date_confidence: disputed: English Wikipedia gives c.1028, Orderic Vitalis implies 1026 or 1027, standard biographers print 1027 or 1028; no month or day is recorded
stops.campa: In the ducal castle above the Ante, Herleva bears Duke Robert a son the church cannot call an heir and Normandy will obey anyway. No contemporary source names the year with confidence and none names the room. Falaise is a frontier keep looking south toward Maine, and the boy is born into the arithmetic of that frontier: which baron holds which valley, and which castellan can be trusted through a winter. Orderic will call his mother a tanner's daughter; historians read the word another way and note that her family stood too high for the trade. The insult will be shouted at him from a wall regardless.
suggested_refs: The Château de Falaise; the standing keep is twelfth and thirteenth century work, later than anything William saw

stops.name: Rouen, the child recognized as duke
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1035; Robert dies at Nicaea in July and the month of the recognition at Rouen is not given
stops.campa: In January the duke had gathered his magnates and made them swear fealty to the boy before setting out for Jerusalem. In July he dies at Nicaea on the road home, and the oath comes due on a child of seven or eight. Rouen receives him as duke in the ducal palace by the Seine, the capital of a duchy whose barons have just been handed a minority to feed on. Above the city on the côte, the relic cult of Catherine of Alexandria is already keeping her name in Norman ground. Four centuries on, this same city will hold the trial of Joan of Arc and pay for her with the taxes of a conquered Normandy.
suggested_refs: The ducal palace at Rouen; the abbey of Holy Trinity on the Côte Sainte-Catherine, enshrining the relics brought by the viscount Goscelin
sources: William of Jumièges, Gesta Normannorum Ducum

stops.name: Le Vaudreuil, the guardians murdered
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: tradition places one plot on the boy duke's household here in the 1040s; the chroniclers disagree on the sequence and the sites of the minority killings
stops.campa: The duchy eats its own regents. Archbishop Robert of Rouen, the strongest protector, is dead in 1037, and after him the guardians and tutors go one at a time, knifed at night or taken in ambush, and in some tellings killed in the room where the boy sleeps. Tradition puts one such plot at Vaudreuil on the Eure. Orderic supplies the murders and the chroniclers cannot be made to agree on their order, so a single place stands here for a decade of them. William survives it by being moved between households and hidden inside them, learning early what a Norman oath is worth without a sword behind it.
suggested_refs: The Château de Vaudreuil on the Eure, one of the traditional sites of the minority assassinations

stops.name: Valognes, the night ride
stops.date_confidence: attested by William of Poitiers as an event; dated 1046 or early 1047 by different sources, month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: In the Cotentin, at Valognes, someone wakes him with the news that the conspirators mean to take him that night. He does not wait for an escort. He rides out alone in the dark, south and east across the peninsula, fords the Vire, and comes to Falaise at daylight with the horse spent. From his birth castle he sends to Henry I of France, his overlord, for an army. The flight is the hinge: the boy who has been carried from house to house for eleven years has just chosen, for the first time, where he will be and who will come to him.
suggested_refs: The night road from Valognes to Falaise, the ride that opens William's own account of his rule

stops.name: Val-ès-Dunes, the rebel barons broken
stops.date_confidence: traditional: 10 August is conventional and Wikipedia notes there is no decisive evidence for it; Douglas argues early 1047, Bates summer 1047
stops.campa: On the open chalk plain east of Caen the French king's horse and the duke's own men meet the coalition of Cotentin and Bessin barons who have decided a bastard of nineteen is a vacancy. The rebels break and are drowned in numbers crossing the Orne. William is not yet master of Normandy but no one will assemble against him on that scale again. He follows the victory with the Truce of God proclaimed through the duchy, forbidding private war on the days the church names, and so takes the first thing a duke needs after an army: the right to say when other men may fight.
suggested_refs: The Val-ès-Dunes plain near Conteville and Vimont, Calvados; the Truce of God promulgated in Normandy after the battle

stops.name: Brionne, Guy of Burgundy besieged out
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1050 as the siege's end; the siege runs for years and its start is not fixed
stops.campa: Guy of Burgundy, the duke's own cousin and the man the rebels wanted in his place, holds the stone hall on the island in the Risle. William does not storm it. He builds two forts facing the castle, sits down in front of them, and waits out the years it takes. Guy is starved into terms and sent out of Normandy. He will fight this way for forty years: the long siege preferred to the battle, the beaten man left alive and landless rather than made a martyr. The ground is what he keeps.
suggested_refs: The donjon of Brionne on the Risle, held against William by Guy of Burgundy

stops.name: Alençon, the hides on the walls
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1051; the Domfront siege of the same campaign runs 1051-52
stops.campa: Alençon holds for Geoffrey Martel of Anjou on the southern march, and its garrison beats hides over the palisade and shouts about the tanner as the duke's column comes up. He takes the town and has the hands and feet of the mockers cut off in sight of the walls. Domfront, besieged in the same campaign, hears about it and comes to terms. The chroniclers who admire him record the mutilation without apology; it is how a frontier is taught. His mother's ancestry is disputed by historians and was never disputed by the men on that wall.
suggested_refs: The walls of Alençon and the castle of Domfront, the two sieges that fixed Normandy's southern frontier

stops.name: Eu, the forbidden marriage
stops.date_confidence: disputed: the chronology lens gives 1051, Wikipedia gives 'early 1050s', the Matilda of Flanders article gives c.1051-52; papal approval comes only from Nicholas II in 1059
stops.campa: Pope Leo IX had forbidden the match at the Council of Rheims in October 1049, citing kinship. William marries Matilda of Flanders anyway, at Eu on the Norman border, and gains with her the alliance of the count of Flanders on his eastern flank. Rome takes eight years to accept the fact, and the price of acceptance is two abbeys at Caen, his and hers, raised as penance for a marriage neither of them undid. The papal prohibition he overrode in 1051 does not stop him applying for a papal banner in 1066, and it is granted.
suggested_refs: Notre-Dame d'Eu, traditional site of the marriage; the papal objection recorded at the Council of Reims, 1049

stops.name: Mortemer, the victory he did not win
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1054; the chronology lens wrongly places William at the battle, the geography lens correctly does not
stops.campa: Henry I of France invades in two columns, and the northern one is caught quartered and drunk at Mortemer in the Bray country. Robert of Eu, Walter Giffard, William de Warenne, Roger of Mortemer and Hugh of Gournay destroy it there. The duke is not present: he is west of the Seine, holding the other column off in person. The canon gives him the day anyway, because a lord is his men. The lesson he takes from it is that the king of France can be beaten by Normans while the duke is somewhere else, and he spends the rest of his life arranging that.
suggested_refs: The Mortemer-sur-Eaulne battlefield, February 1054, won by William's barons in his absence

stops.name: Varaville, the river takes the French
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1057; the month is given as August by convention and the day is not recorded
stops.campa: Henry and Geoffrey Martel come again, plundering through the Hiémois, and turn for home across the Dives at Varaville. William waits until half the army is over and the tide is turning in the estuary, then falls on the rearguard trapped on the wrong bank with the water rising behind it. The king watches his own men destroyed from the far side and cannot cross back. It is the third French invasion and the last. Three years later Henry and Geoffrey are both dead within months of each other, and no power on the continent is left that can order the duke of Normandy to stop.
suggested_refs: The ford and marsh of the Dives estuary at Varaville

stops.name: Caen, the donjon above the two rivers
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the castle is dated c.1060 from the archaeological record; no foundation act survives
stops.campa: On the rock between the Orne and the Odon he raises a great stone castle, and around it a town that is his own work rather than an inheritance. Rouen is the old capital, ecclesiastical, Roman-founded, full of men whose families were there before his. Caen is new ground, and he builds it as a second seat: a ducal hall, quarried stone that will be shipped to England for a century, two abbeys going up at either end of it. A ruler who has spent his childhood being moved between other men's houses builds himself a city.
suggested_refs: The donjon of the Château de Caen; the Caen limestone quarries that later supply English cathedral building
sources: archaeological record of the Caen donjon

stops.name: Caen, Saint-Étienne founded as penance
stops.date_confidence: attested: founded 1063, construction begins 1066, dedication 1077; one research lens wrongly compressed this to a consecration in 1063
stops.campa: The abbey of Saint-Étienne is founded at the west end of Caen as the man's half of the penance for the marriage Rome refused, Matilda raising the Abbaye aux Dames at the other end of the town. Building starts in the year he sails for England, and the church is not dedicated until 1077, by which time the founder is a king. He endows it richly and means to be buried in it. He will be, twenty-four years on, in front of a congregation that leaves the church before the grave is closed.
stops.quote: He died in Normandy the day after the nativity of St. Mary, and he was buried in Caen, at St. Stephen's monastery, which he had built and had richly endowed.
stops.quote_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal 1087, trans. J. A. Giles (Wikisource, djvu/177)
suggested_refs: The Abbaye aux Hommes (Saint-Étienne) and the Abbaye aux Dames at Caen, the paired penitential foundations

stops.name: Bosham, Harold takes ship
stops.date_confidence: the Tapestry names Bosham and William of Poitiers gives no departure point; the voyage is dated 1064 by English tradition and 1065 by French Wikipedia following Poitiers
stops.campa: Earl Harold Godwinson eats in the hall at his Sussex manor, walks down to the water, and sails. Why he sails, no one can now establish: to ransom kinsmen, to hunt, to treat with the duke, or driven out by weather on a coastal trip. The Bayeux Tapestry, made for the winning side, shows the departure as the first panel of a story whose ending it already knows. The wind takes him across and puts him on the wrong shore, in Ponthieu, where wrecked men belong by custom to the count who finds them.
suggested_refs: Holy Trinity church at Bosham, shown in the opening scenes of the Bayeux Tapestry

stops.name: Beaurain, the shipwrecked earl held
stops.date_confidence: attested as an episode by William of Poitiers and the Tapestry; no month is recorded and the year follows the disputed dating of the voyage
stops.campa: Count Guy of Ponthieu takes the wreck and its passenger and holds the greatest earl in England at Beaurain on the Canche, waiting to be paid. William, as Guy's overlord, does not offer a ransom. He sends and demands the man. Guy hands him over and rides with him to the Norman border. The most powerful subject of the English king enters Normandy as a guest who cannot leave, and everything he does for the next months is done inside that fact. The Tapestry shows the handover without comment on it.
suggested_refs: Beaurainville on the Canche, Pas-de-Calais, where Count Guy held Harold

stops.name: Dol-de-Bretagne, the Breton campaign with Harold
stops.date_confidence: attested to the same visit as the oath; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: The duke takes his guest to war. The campaign runs into Brittany against Conan II, and the Tapestry shows Harold fighting at William's side and hauling men out of the quicksands at the Couesnon under the Mount. Arms are given, and in Norman law a man who takes arms from a lord has taken something else with them. Harold is being shown the Norman army from the inside, and he is being made, panel by panel, into a member of it. Twenty-eight months later he will meet the same army on a hill in Sussex.
suggested_refs: The Breton campaign of 1064 against Conan II, shown in the Bayeux Tapestry from Mont-Saint-Michel to Dinan

stops.name: Bonneville-sur-Touques, the oath on the relics
stops.date_confidence: site disputed: William of Poitiers says Bonneville, the Bayeux Tapestry says Bayeux, and the sources are not reconciled; date disputed 1064 or 1065; the terms sworn are Norman testimony uncorroborated by any English source
stops.campa: Harold puts his hands on relics and swears. What he swears is the whole Norman case for 1066, and it survives only in the mouths of the men who won. William of Poitiers puts the scene at Bonneville; Odo's tapestry puts it at Bayeux; the English chroniclers do not record the terms at all. Under two reliquaries, some of them concealed until afterward in the version the Normans liked best, an earl who cannot go home unless he swears something swears it. He then goes home, and in January the witan gives him the crown.
suggested_refs: The Château de Bonneville-sur-Touques and the Bayeux Tapestry oath panel, two irreconcilable sites for one oath

stops.name: Lillebonne, the barons argued into an invasion
stops.date_confidence: attested to early 1066 by Orderic and Wace; no precise date survives
stops.campa: Edward dies at Westminster on the fifth of January and Harold is crowned there on the sixth, the day of the funeral. The news reaches Normandy and William calls his magnates to the old Roman-walled town of Lillebonne above the Seine. They are not obliged to follow him overseas and they know it; Wace remembers them arguing it out in groups before agreeing man by man, each for a stated number of ships. Rome sends a banner. What the hall agrees to is a shareholding, and every baron in it is buying English land with hulls.
suggested_refs: The castle and council hall at Lillebonne, where the Norman magnates agreed ship quotas for the invasion

stops.name: Dives-sur-Mer, the fleet and the wind
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1066; the fleet's arrival at the Dives is dated to the summer without a precise day
stops.campa: Through the late summer the ships gather at the mouth of the Dives and cannot go. Horses have to be fed on the beach for weeks, discipline held over an idle army of hired men from Brittany, Flanders and Boulogne, and the whole enterprise costs money every day it does not sail. Harold's fleet waits opposite until its provisions run out and it disbands in early September. In the same decade other Norman knights are riding into Apulia and Sicily under the Hautevilles, and Morgan le Fay's cult will follow them to Etna. The wind is the only thing in Europe that does not answer to Normans.
suggested_refs: The estuary of the Dives, mustering ground of the 1066 fleet; the nineteenth-century Dives monument listing William's supposed companions

stops.name: Stamford Bridge, the other invasion
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Two hundred miles north of where the Normans will land, Harold Godwinson destroys the last Viking army to come for England. Harald Hardrada of Norway and Tostig, Harold's own brother, are killed, and the Norse survivors need twenty-four ships to carry home what came in three hundred. It is the most complete English victory of the century and it is fought four days before William's keels touch Sussex sand. The English king now has a wrecked army, a forced march the length of the kingdom, and no fleet in the Channel.
suggested_refs: The crossing of the Derwent at Stamford Bridge, Yorkshire

stops.name: Saint-Valery-sur-Somme, the relics carried out
stops.date_confidence: attested: the fleet embarks on 27 September and lands on 28 September
stops.campa: Storm drives the fleet up the coast into Ponthieu and holds it there weeks longer, men drowned on the way and buried quietly so the army does not count them. At Saint-Valery the duke has the bones of the local saint carried out of the church and paraded before the host to pray for wind. The wind comes that night. They embark in the dark, the duke's ship lit at the masthead so the rest can follow, and by the accounts the Mora outruns the fleet and has to lie to at dawn waiting for it.
suggested_refs: The relics of Saint Valery, paraded before the fleet at Saint-Valery-sur-Somme

stops.name: Pevensey, the landing
stops.date_confidence: the landing is attested; the stumble and the grasped earth are legendary, a topos also told of Julius Caesar, and the quoted words are Wace's twelfth-century verse, not a chronicle record
stops.campa: The fleet comes in unopposed inside the Roman shore fort at Pevensey, and the army throws up a camp within the old walls the same day. The story is that the duke slips coming out of the boat and fills his hands with the shingle. Malmesbury gives the line to a soldier standing near, and doubts the whole tale on the grounds that his chaplain, who was there, says nothing of it. Wace gives it to William himself, in verse, a century after. The atlas keeps the legend where the legend belongs, in the mouth of the poet who wrote it.
stops.quote: But he cried out lustily, "See, seignors, by the splendour of God! I have seized England with my two hands; without challenge no prize can be made; all is our own that is here..."
stops.quote_source: Wace, Roman de Rou, trans. Edgar Taylor, Master Wace, His Chronicle of the Norman Conquest (1837), pp. 130-131
suggested_refs: The Roman shore fort at Pevensey, Anderitum, reused as the Norman beachhead
sources: William of Malmesbury, Chronicle of the Kings of England, trans. Giles, Book III, p. 274

stops.name: Senlac Hill, the battle at Hastings
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He has moved his army east to Hastings and raised a prefabricated motte there, burning the country around it until the English king has to come to him. Harold comes on the fourteenth with an army that marched from Yorkshire, and puts it on the ridge in shield wall. The fight lasts the whole day, which almost no medieval battle does. Feigned flights pull the English line open, the arrows come down, Harold is killed with his two brothers, and by dusk the kingdom has no royal house left standing that can field a man. The Normans hold the field and count.
stops.quote: This king William, of whom we are speaking, was a very wise and a great man, and more honoured and more powerful than any of his predecessors. He was mild to those good men who loved God, but severe beyond measure towards those who withstood his will.
stops.quote_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal 1087, trans. J. A. Giles (Wikisource, djvu/177)
suggested_refs: Senlac Hill and the high altar of Battle Abbey, sited by tradition where Harold fell

stops.name: Dover, the town burned
stops.date_confidence: attested to late October 1066; the exact day is not recorded
stops.campa: He does not march on London. He turns along the coast, taking the ports that could bring another army over, and Dover surrenders at sight of him. His men fire part of the town anyway, and he pays compensation for the houses, which the chroniclers note as remarkable. Then he fortifies the cliff and sits eight days while dysentery goes through the army. After Hastings the conquest proceeds as a slow closing of the country's doors, one port and one river crossing at a time, and hardly any of it is fought.
suggested_refs: The cliff-top fortification at Dover, first of the Norman works on the Kent coast

stops.name: Canterbury, the submission and the sickness
stops.date_confidence: attested to the advance of late 1066; no precise date
stops.campa: Canterbury submits as he comes up, the seat of the English church changing sides without a siege. There he falls seriously ill and the advance stops for weeks while the duke of Normandy lies in the primatial city of a kingdom he has won one battle in and cannot yet leave. He recovers. Within four years the archbishopric will be taken from Stigand and given to Lanfranc of Pavia, and the English church will be run by men who learned their law abroad. The conquest of the altar takes longer than the conquest of the fields and it is more thorough.
suggested_refs: Canterbury, submitted 1066; the see given to Lanfranc in 1070

stops.name: Wallingford, Stigand at the ford
stops.date_confidence: attested to the encirclement of London in late 1066; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: London is walled and holds Edgar Ætheling, whom the city has proclaimed king. William does not assault it. He burns Southwark, then swings west in a wide arc through Hampshire and Berkshire, cutting the city off from the country that feeds it, and crosses the Thames at Wallingford. There Archbishop Stigand, who crowned Harold, comes out and submits to him and abandons Edgar. The encirclement takes about six weeks and costs him almost nothing. The city surrenders itself.
suggested_refs: The Thames crossing at Wallingford, where Stigand submitted

stops.name: Berkhamsted, the crown offered
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1066; the day is not fixed in the sources
stops.campa: At Berkhamsted north of London the remnant of English government comes out to him: Edgar Ætheling, the boy they had elected six weeks earlier, Archbishop Ealdred of York, the bishops, the earls Edwin and Morcar, the citizens of London. They give hostages, they swear, and they offer him the crown. He accepts. The Chronicle records the submission and then records that his men went on plundering all the same. The kingship he takes at Berkhamsted is, in its own legal telling, given to him by the English, which is exactly the form the Norman case has needed since Bonneville.
suggested_refs: Berkhamsted, site of the English submission and of the Norman motte raised after it

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, crowned among burning houses
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ealdred of York crowns him in Edward's new church on Christmas Day, eleven months after Harold was crowned on the same stone. The congregation is asked in English and in French whether it accepts him, and the shout that answers is heard outside by the Norman guard, who take it for a rising and set fire to the houses around the abbey. The church empties into the smoke. He is left at the altar with a few clergy, finishing the rite. The English of the writs and the law courts begins its slow eclipse here; nine centuries later Tolkien will hold a chair at Oxford in what it became.
stops.quote: any man, who was himself aught, might travel over the kingdom with a bosom-full of gold unmolested
stops.quote_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal 1087, trans. J. A. Giles (Wikisource, djvu/178)
suggested_refs: Edward the Confessor's Westminster Abbey, consecrated 1065, the coronation church of both kings of 1066

stops.name: Exeter, Rougemont, eighteen days
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged: the chronology lens dates the siege to December 1067, the geography lens to 1068; the return from Normandy is December 1067 and the siege is early 1068
stops.campa: Exeter refuses to admit his officers or to swear more than the tribute it paid earlier kings, and Harold's mother Gytha is inside the walls. He brings up an army including English levies, blinds a hostage in front of the gate, and sits down for eighteen days until the city comes out. Gytha escapes by sea. He builds Rougemont in the corner of the Roman wall before he leaves, and the west is held. The pattern is set for a generation: a rising, a siege, a castle left standing in the town that rose.
stops.quote: The king was also of great sternness, and he took from his subjects many marks of gold, and many hundred pounds of silver, and this, either with or without right, and with little need. He was given to avarice, and greedily loved gain.
stops.quote_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal 1087, trans. J. A. Giles (Wikisource, djvu/178)
suggested_refs: Rougemont Castle, Exeter, raised in the angle of the Roman city wall after the eighteen-day siege

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, Matilda crowned queen
stops.date_confidence: attested to 11 May 1068 at Westminster by the Archbishop of York; the chronology lens wrongly gives Winchester
stops.campa: Matilda of Flanders comes over and is crowned queen at Pentecost by Ealdred of York, in the church where her husband was crowned seventeen months before. The marriage Rome forbade now holds two crowns. She has governed Normandy in his absence and will do so again for years at a stretch, with their son Robert nominally beside her, and the Conquest is administered from two capitals by two people who between them are never in the same country for long. Their fourth son, Henry, is born in England within the next three years, the only one of them born to a king.
suggested_refs: The Pentecost coronation of Matilda of Flanders, Westminster Abbey, 11 May 1068

stops.name: York, the crown worn in the ruins
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The north has risen twice in one year. Edgar Ætheling attacked York in the spring, came back in the autumn with a Danish fleet under Sweyn's brother, and the city and both its new castles were taken and their garrisons killed. William buys the Danes off, retakes the burnt city, and has his crown and his regalia brought north from Winchester so that he can wear them at the Christmas mass in the wreck of York. There is almost no city left to be crowned in. He sits in it in the vestments anyway, which is the whole argument.
suggested_refs: The two Norman castles at York, taken and burnt in 1069; the site of Clifford's Tower

stops.name: York, the Harrying of the North
stops.date_confidence: attested as a campaign of the winter of 1069-70; the casualty figure is Orderic's own estimate, written half a century later
stops.campa: Through the winter his companies move out from York across Yorkshire and beyond it, burning villages, granaries, ploughs and cattle, and salting nothing because there is no need. Men who survive the fire starve in February. Sixteen years later the Domesday clerks will still be writing the word waste beside hundreds of northern manors. He then swings west through the Pennines in the same season and builds castles at Chester and Stafford. Orderic Vitalis, who grew up under Norman rule and admires him elsewhere, refuses to defend this.
stops.quote: more than a hundred thousand souls, of both sexes and all ages, perished of want. On many occasions, in the course of the present history, I have been free to extol William according to his merits, but I dare not commend him for an act which levelled both the bad and the good together in one common ruin, by the infliction of a consuming famine.
stops.quote_source: Orderic Vitalis, Historia Ecclesiastica, Book IV, trans. Thomas Forester, The Ecclesiastical History of England and Normandy, vol. 2 (1854), p. 28
suggested_refs: The waste entries for Yorkshire in Domesday Book, the administrative trace of the harrying
sources: Orderic Vitalis, trans. Forester, vol. 2, p. 28

stops.name: Winchester, the legates crown him again
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Easter court of 1070; the day is calculated from the date of Easter, not given by the sources
stops.campa: Papal legates come to the Easter court at Winchester and crown him a second time, this time with Rome's own hands on the diadem, and then sit as a council and begin taking the English church apart. Stigand is deposed and imprisoned, and other native bishops with him. Lanfranc of Bec goes to Canterbury and Thomas of Bayeux to York. Within a decade almost no Englishman holds a see or a great abbey. Battle Abbey is founded the same year on the ridge where Harold fell, its high altar set on the spot, a penance and a title deed in one building.
suggested_refs: The Easter council of Winchester, 1070; the foundation of Battle Abbey on the field of Hastings

stops.name: Ely, the causeway over the fen
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1071; no month recorded. Earl Edwin's death in the same year belongs to the road to Scotland, not to Ely, though one research lens welded the two together
stops.campa: The last English resistance is water. Hereward and Earl Morcar hold the island in the fen at Ely, where an army cannot deploy and boats cannot be massed. William has a causeway built out across the marsh, and the sources add a witch set on a tower to curse the defenders, which is what a besieging army tells itself when it is standing in mud. Ely falls, Morcar goes to prison for life, Hereward vanishes into legend. Edwin, his brother, is killed the same year by his own retinue on the road north to Scotland, and the old earldoms end.
suggested_refs: The causeway across the fen to the Isle of Ely; the Liber Eliensis account, late and part legend

stops.name: Abernethy, Malcolm becomes his man
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1072; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: Malcolm III of Scotland has married Edgar Ætheling's sister and has been raiding into a north William already burned. So the king marches an army up past the Forth with a fleet on his flank, finds nothing to fight, and gets what he came for at Abernethy on the Tay: Malcolm becomes his man, gives hostages including his own son, and puts Edgar out of Scotland. No battle is recorded. Six years after Hastings the frontier of the English kingdom is settled by a Scottish king's oath, and the conquest is over as a war.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Abernethy, 1072, on the Tay

segments.name: The Rear Door: Maine, Brittany, and a Son

stops.name: Le Mans, Maine retaken
stops.date_confidence: attested to March 1073
stops.campa: While he was busy in England, Maine threw the Normans out and set up a commune with Angevin backing. He comes back across the Channel with an English army, which is the new arithmetic of his life, and takes Le Mans in March. English soldiers are now used to hold a French county for a Norman duke who is a king somewhere else. Every year after this the two halves pull against each other: a rising in England while he is in Normandy, a war in Maine while he is in England, and the sea in between taking weeks he does not have.
suggested_refs: Le Mans and the county of Maine, held for Normandy by an army raised in England

stops.name: Winchester, Waltheof beheaded
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1076; the day 31 May is the conventional date
stops.campa: The Revolt of the Earls in 1075 was made by Normans and Bretons, Ralph de Gael and Roger de Breteuil, not by the English. Waltheof, the one English earl left, was told of it, kept silent, then confessed it to Lanfranc and to the king. Roger is imprisoned for life. Waltheof is taken outside Winchester at first light and beheaded, the only English noble William executes in twenty-one years. Crowds come to his grave at Crowland and call him a martyr, and miracles are reported there within a few years.
stops.quote: he kept in prison those earls who acted against his pleasure; he removed bishops from their sees, and abbats from their offices
stops.quote_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal 1087, trans. J. A. Giles (Wikisource, djvu/177-178)
suggested_refs: The execution site outside Winchester and the cult of Waltheof at Crowland Abbey

stops.name: Dol, driven off by the king of France
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1076
stops.campa: He besieges Dol in Brittany, the same border town he campaigned around with Harold twelve years earlier, and this time Philip I of France brings an army up and breaks the siege. William withdraws with heavy losses in men, horses and treasure. It is one of the few clear defeats of his life and it happens at fifty, against a king twenty-five years his junior who has learned what Henry I never learned: that Normandy is only unbeatable when the duke is allowed to fight one enemy at a time.
suggested_refs: The castle of Dol-de-Bretagne, relieved by Philip I in September 1076

stops.name: Gerberoy, unhorsed by his own son
stops.date_confidence: attested to late January or early February 1079; the recognition of his father's voice is Orderic's telling and is [R]
stops.campa: Robert Curthose, the eldest son, wants Normandy now rather than at his father's death, and Philip of France gives him the castle of Gerberoy on the Beauvais border to raise war from. The king besieges it and the garrison comes out. In the fighting Robert wounds his father in the hand and puts him on the ground, and the story is that he knew the voice under the helmet and gave him a horse to get away on. William's second son is wounded in the same fight. He curses Robert publicly and is reconciled to him a year later, and curses him again on his deathbed.
suggested_refs: Gerberoy in the Oise, held for Robert Curthose against his father in 1079

segments.name: The Book and the Seven Feet

stops.name: Gloucester, the survey commissioned
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Christmas court of 1085
stops.campa: A Danish invasion is expected, mercenaries have been quartered on the country all year, and money has to be found. At the Christmas court at Gloucester the king holds what the Chronicle calls deep speech with his council, and sends men into every shire to write down who holds what, how many ploughs, how many mills, how many head, what it was worth in King Edward's day and what it is worth now. Nothing like it has been attempted in Europe since Rome. The English call the result Domesday because there is no appeal from it.
stops.quote: So very narrowly he caused it to be investigated, that there was not one single hide, nor one yard of land, nor even, it is shame to tell, though it seemed to him no shame to do, an ox, nor a cow, nor a pig, was left, that was not set down in his writ.
suggested_refs: The Christmas court of 1085 at Gloucester; the Exchequer Domesday volumes

stops.name: Old Sarum, the oath of every landholder
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 August 1086
stops.campa: On the first of August every man of property in England worth summoning comes to the hill fort above Salisbury, tenants of the crown and tenants of other men alike, and each of them swears fealty to the king directly, over the head of whatever lord he holds his land from. It cancels the whole logic of a subinfeudated kingdom in one afternoon. The returns of the survey are being compiled at Winchester in the same months. He now knows what every one of these men has, and he has their oath, and there is nothing between him and any of them.
stops.quote: He reigned over England, and being sharp-sighted to his own interest, he surveyed the kingdom so thoroughly that there was not a single hide of land throughout the whole, of which he knew not the possessor, and how much it was worth, and this he afterwards entered in his register.
stops.quote_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal 1087, trans. J. A. Giles (Wikisource, djvu/178)
suggested_refs: The Iron Age ramparts of Old Sarum, site of the Salisbury Oath of 1 August 1086

stops.name: Mantes-la-Jolie, the town burned
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1087; the Chronicle dates the campaign before the Assumption, that is before 15 August, without a day
stops.campa: The French Vexin is the corridor between Rouen and Paris, chalk bends of the Seine where Clotilde once founded her house of virgins at Andely. Philip of France holds it and jokes about the Norman king's belly. William burns Mantes with its churches and two anchorites inside them. Riding through the burning streets his horse rears or stumbles on hot ash and throws him forward onto the iron pommel of the saddle, and something tears inside him. He is carried back to Rouen. The last thing he does as a soldier is a raid, and the raid kills him.
stops.quote: The same year also, before the assumption of St. Mary, king William marched with an army out of Normandy into France, and made war upon his own lord king Philip, and slew a great number of his people, and burned the town of Mante, and all the holy monasteries in it, and two holy men who served God as anchorites were burned there.
stops.quote_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal 1087, trans. J. A. Giles (Wikisource, djvu/176)
suggested_refs: Mantes on the Seine, burnt in the summer of 1087; the Vexin corridor between Rouen and Paris

stops.name: Rouen, Saint-Gervais, death outside the walls
stops.date_confidence: attested to 9 September 1087 at the priory of Saint-Gervais extra muros; two research lenses gave coordinates 600 m and 1.4 km off, both corrected here
stops.campa: The noise of the city disturbs him, so they carry him out to the priory of Saint-Gervais on the hill west of the walls. He lies there some weeks, dividing the inheritance: Normandy to Robert who fought him, England to William Rufus, five thousand pounds of silver to Henry who will outlive both. He orders his English prisoners released and endows the churches of Mantes he burned. Orderic, writing thirty-five years later, puts a long confession in his mouth. He dies at first light. The attendants strip the room of everything portable and leave the body on the floor.
stops.quote: These events inflamed me to the highest pitch of resentment, and I fell on the English of the northern counties like a raving lion. I commanded their houses and corn, with all their implements and furniture, to be burnt without distinction, and large herds of cattle and beasts of burden, to be butchered wherever they were found.
stops.quote_source: Orderic Vitalis, Historia Ecclesiastica, Book VII ch. XV, trans. Thomas Forester, vol. 2 (1854), pp. 412-413; the deathbed speech is Orderic's own composition, not a transcript
suggested_refs: The priory church of Saint-Gervais at Rouen, built extra muros, a ducal residence and the place of William's death
sources: Orderic Vitalis, trans. Forester, vol. 2, pp. 412-413

stops.name: Caen, the tomb too small
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1087; the day of the funeral is not fixed
stops.campa: A country knight pays out of his own purse for the body to go down the Seine and along the coast to Caen. A fire breaks out in the town during the procession and the mourners leave to fight it. At the graveside a citizen named Ascelin stops the service to say the abbey stands on his father's land, taken without payment, and has to be paid there and then. Then the stone coffin proves too short for the swollen corpse; forcing it down bursts the body, and the stench empties the church of the men who came to bury the king of England.
stops.quote: Oh, how false, how unstable, is the good of this world! He, who had been a powerful king and the lord of many territories, possessed not then, of all his lands, more than seven feet of ground.
stops.quote_source: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, annal 1087, trans. J. A. Giles (Wikisource, djvu/177)
suggested_refs: The choir of Saint-Étienne de Caen, William's own foundation and his grave

stops.name: Caen, the bones scattered
stops.date_confidence: the sequence 1522, 1562, 1642, c.1742, 1793 is uncontested in outline but rests on unnamed nineteenth-century Norman antiquarian histories that could not be reached; what survives today is disputed
stops.campa: The tomb is opened in 1522 on papal authorization and the skeleton is reported whole, wrapped in leather, and sealed up again with a new inscription. In 1562 Huguenot soldiers break it open and throw the bones out; one thighbone is picked up and kept. It goes back under a new monument in 1642, and the grander monument raised about 1742 is destroyed in its turn by revolutionary mobs in 1793. A white marble ledger stone of the early nineteenth century covers the place now. Whether anything of him is beneath it, the local histories contradict each other.
suggested_refs: The nineteenth-century ledger stone in the choir of Saint-Étienne, fifth marker over the grave
sources: Abbaye aux Hommes chapter records cited in Norman antiquarian histories

stops.name: Falaise, the bronze horseman above Rollo
stops.date_confidence: attested as a monument of 1851 by Louis Rochet; the reading of its programme is interpretation
stops.campa: Louis Rochet's equestrian bronze goes up in the square below the castle in 1851, the duke mounted and armed, and around the plinth in stone the six dukes before him from Rollo the Norseman onward. The town that could not say which room he was born in builds the lineage in stone instead, and the conquest becomes the last term in a series rather than the act of one bastard with an army of shareholders. Richard the Lionheart, five generations on, will be spoken of as sitting on his own throne at Caen; the throne is this one.
suggested_refs: Louis Rochet's 1851 equestrian statue, Place Guillaume-le-Conquérant, Falaise; the Bayeux Tapestry, whose Kentish or Norman making is still disputed
